From the homes already running Nubo.
Real homes have been living with Nubo for months. Here's what the first testers make of it.
Part of the beta program? Tell us how Nubo is settling in.
"It took the dog three days. It took my husband three weeks."

We expected a gadget. What we got was closer to a very polite housemate who happens to be excellent at finding lost things. My husband came around — mostly since it started remembering where he leaves his glasses.
"It knows my daughter better than I remembered to."
She likes the blinds half-open, I like them shut. Nubo picked up on both within a week and stopped asking. I've lived with people who took longer to learn that.
"My kids named it before I did."

It's Barnaby now, apparently, and there's no walking that back. What surprised me wasn't the tech, it was how fast it stopped feeling like tech. Three weeks in, it's just the thing that gets the door.
"I braced for another device to babysit."

Instead I got a system that runs itself. No app I have to open, no light that blinks until I pay attention to it. It does the job and gets out of the room, which is more than I can say for most of my houseguests.
"Six weeks in, and the novelty still hasn't worn off — because there wasn't much novelty to wear off."
It doesn't do tricks. It clears the table, it charges itself, it stays out of the kitchen when we're cooking. My last three smart home purchases wanted applause. This one just wants a dock.
"The first robot I've owned that doesn't ask to be noticed."
That's rarer than it sounds. Everything else in this house beeps, glows, or asks me to rate my experience. Nubo has opinions about none of that. It just does the thing and moves on.
You'll wonder how the house ran without it.

title: Nubo — One product, done right.
text: We would rather get one thing right.
Nubo is a home robot. It learns how a household actually runs, then takes the small daily work off your hands without asking for your attention in return.
We are fourteen people across two studios. The shell is knitted in Como. The behavior is built in Cambridge. Between them, one product, currently living in 140 homes.

Every robot we tested wanted to be the center of the room. Screens, chimes, a wake word repeated until it listened. We kept thinking about the opposite. A machine that earns its place by asking for nothing.

So we started with behavior instead of features. What should it do on its own. When should it wait. What does it never interrupt. The hardware came after the manners. Three years later, Nubo is the result.
If a feature exists to demo well rather than help daily, it does not ship. We killed half the list this way and the product got better each time.
Nubo observes and moves without announcing itself. No wake word, no chime, no light asking to be looked at. Silence is the resting state.
Perception runs on the device. Nothing it sees or hears leaves the house to make the product work, and there is a shutter you can close over the lens.
Nubo v0.1, drawn before a single part was machined.
Every behavior is argued out here before it reaches a home.

text: Nubo is in beta. This is where the work shows, as it ships.
No tiers locked behind subscriptions. The robot is yours. The care plan is optional.
A note when something ships. Nothing else.
One hundred and forty homes, and counting.

The beta crossed 140 households this week. Enough range now to see how Nubo behaves in small flats and full houses alike, and enough data to stop guessing about a few things we had been guessing about.
Nubo now learns quiet hours on its own.
It used to wait to be told when the house sleeps. Now it watches the first week and works it out. Movement slows, tasks pause, and it holds until morning without a schedule set by hand.
Steadier hands near the small stuff.
Grip response is smoother at the light end of the range. Picking up a single Lego or a full glass now reads the same to Nubo. Force sensing got a little more patient.
The dock no longer sulks in bright light.
Direct sun near the dock used to confuse the return sensor, and Nubo would circle before settling. It reads the glare correctly now and parks on the first pass.
A second beta wave opens in August.
We are opening a second wave of the beta next month, with room for a few hundred more homes. If you are on the waitlist, keep an eye on your inbox.
